newsitem.title: USA: Downside pressure on copper prices - Cerro.
newsitem.headline: Downside pressure on copper prices - Cerro.

text.p: Greater mined copper supplies, the solving of current production problems at certain plants and the lack of a rapid short-term increase in demand look set to push red metal prices lower, said Bil Rickher, vice president, raw material, at Cerro Copper Products Co.
"There is more downside potential than upside," Rickher told delegates at the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries Round Table here.
Rickher said that despite the Federal Reserve's decision to leave interest rates unchanged on Tuesday, there was still upside pressure on rates.

Copper supplies will also be greater than demand over the next few years, suppressing the price of copper. Although the U.S. market was healthy, other regions were not. "Germany, Japan and China don't have the short term potential increase in demand to offset the increase in supply," Rickher said.
Cerro is the world's largest producer of copper tubing, a producer of copper cathode and major consumer of copper scrap.
The scrap market also faced challenges, with the No.1 grade set to feel stiffer competition from electrowon copper metal rather than blister.

Many of the new copper projects, especially in Latin America, will produce low cost copper cathode produced by the solvent extraction, electrowinning method (SX/EW) rather than the traditional, and more expensive, copper ore to blister and electrolytic cathode route.

"Most of the electrolytic cathode will be destined for wire rod production. The biggest competitor for No. 1 scrap will be all of the new electrowon cathode that is cheap to produce, and much is not registered for delivery to the market," Rickher said.
"No. 1 will stay in demand but will have to compete on price," he added.

For the No. 2 grade scrap, foreign markets will continue to dictate the domestic price, and the number of U.S. consumers of this grade will dwindle. China has been a large buyer of No. 2 scrap from the United States.

Rickher said that after two years of undercapacity, the copper tube market was heading for overcapacity due to large expansions in the U.S. - some by Cerro itself - and abroad. U.S. exports of copper tube to Mexico were slapped with a 15 percent duty, but there was no duty on exports in the opposite direction.

"I think there will be price cutting and oversupply of tubing," Rickher said. "We might see one or two suppliers less." Cerro, a leading player, was not able to takeover some of its rivals because of potential anti-trust problems, he added.

Although copper prices tumbled from 130 cents per pound in early May to a low of just over 82 cents, and recovering to about 90 cents at present, Rickher said he would not be altering the company's price risk management strategy in the wake of Sumitomo.

Cerro was lucky in having minimum copper inventory just before prices collapsed because the company was building a new plant. "I was just lucky but it caught some of our competition severely," Rickher said.
